branch.title: University Physics as a growing network, with reading text
branch.notes: Routes are AND/single; kind classical/relativistic/quantum/to_*/failed; model nodes flagged postulate.

extra.description: Rounds a value to the nearest power of ten so that very different scales can be compared multiplicatively.
The convention that fixes base quantities and their units and builds every other unit as a product of powers of them.
Read from a clock. SI unit the second, fixed by the caesium-133 hyperfine transition frequency.
Read from a ruler. SI unit the metre, fixed by the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299 792 458 s.
Inertial measure of the amount of matter, read from a balance. SI unit the kilogram, fixed since 2019 through Planck's constant.
Multiplies a quantity by a ratio equal to one, so the number changes and the quantity does not.
Tracks the powers of base dimensions in a quantity; an equation is admissible only if both sides carry the same dimension.
Obtains an order-of-magnitude answer from rough inputs combined in a dimensionally consistent way.
Difference between a measured value and the accepted value; a small discrepancy means high accuracy.
The spread of a measured value; percent uncertainty δA/A·100 % compares it with the value itself. Small spread means high precision.
For products and quotients the percent uncertainties add (to first order), which bounds the uncertainty of a result.
Bookkeeping rule that keeps only the digits supported by the uncertainty of the inputs.
A quantity fixed by one real number and a unit; scalars obey ordinary arithmetic.
A quantity with magnitude and direction; displacement is the model case. Two vectors can be parallel, antiparallel or orthogonal.
Combines vectors head to tail (or by the parallelogram) into a resultant; subtraction adds the antiparallel vector.
Stretches a vector by |α| and reverses it if α < 0; dividing a vector by its magnitude gives a unit vector.

extra.symbol: A⃗ = A_x î + A_y ĵ + A_z k̂
extra.description: Writes a vector in the orthonormal basis of a Cartesian coordinate system; vector equations become one scalar equation per axis.
Locates a point in a plane by its distance from the origin and an angle from the x-axis.
Multiplies two vectors into a scalar, AB cos φ; it projects one vector on another and vanishes for orthogonal vectors.
Multiplies two vectors into a vector perpendicular to both, of magnitude AB sin φ, oriented by the right-hand rule.
Coordinate of the body on an axis of the frame at a given instant.
An origin and axes against which positions are measured, together with a clock.
The kinematic state of a body on a line: its position at every instant.
Change of position between two instants; signed. A total displacement is the sum of successive displacements.
Total length of path covered, never negative; it can exceed the magnitude of the displacement.
Displacement divided by the elapsed time; it depends only on the end points of the interval.
Duration of an interval between two clock readings.
The limit of a difference quotient as the interval shrinks; turns a quantity known at every instant into its rate of change.
Rate of change of position at an instant: the slope of x(t).
Distance traveled divided by elapsed time.
Magnitude of the instantaneous velocity.
Change of velocity divided by elapsed time.
Rate of change of velocity: the slope of v(t) and the second derivative of x(t), which sets the concavity of its graph.
The motion when acceleration does not change: velocity linear and position quadratic in time.
Vertical motion with acceleration −g; Galileo's result that the motion does not depend on the mass.
Acceleration of a body falling near Earth's surface without air resistance: about 9.80 m/s², the same for all bodies at one place.
Accumulates a rate over time; undoes the derivative up to a constant fixed by initial conditions.
Vector from the origin of the frame to the body: r⃗ = x î + y ĵ + z k̂.
The kinematic state in space: the curve traced by the position vector, made of three independent motions along the axes.
Change of the position vector between two instants.
Rate of change of the position vector; tangent to the trajectory.
Rate of change of the velocity vector; in curved motion it has parts across and along the path (total acceleration).
Motion under gravity alone: uniform horizontally, free fall vertically, the two independent.
Time a projectile spends in the air.
Horizontal distance traveled by a projectile landing at its launch height.
The state of a body moving on a circle of radius r: its angle at every instant.
Acceleration toward the centre needed to keep a body on a circle.
Rate at which the angle advances, in rad/s; constant in uniform circular motion.
Rate of change of speed; directed along the path.
Converts positions and velocities between two reference frames in relative motion by adding the frames' relative position and velocity.
Velocity of a body measured in a frame that itself moves.
A push or pull on a body, with magnitude and direction; measured by the stretch of a calibrated spring. SI unit the newton, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
Isolates one body and draws every external force on it as a vector from the body; the starting point of every force problem.
Vector sum of all external forces on a body.
A body keeps its velocity unless a net external force acts; this tendency is inertia, measured by mass.
A frame in which the first law holds; any frame moving at constant velocity relative to one is also inertial.
The net external force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration; one equation per component.
Gravitational force of the Earth on a body near its surface; proportional to mass, unlike mass itself it depends on location.
Forces come in pairs: when A pushes on B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force. The two act on different bodies.
Contact force perpendicular to a surface, as large as needed to stop the body from moving into it.
Pulling force transmitted along a string or cable.
A spring pulls back with a force proportional to its stretch from the relaxed length.
Contact force parallel to a surface that opposes relative motion (kinetic) or its onset (static), proportional to the normal force.
Friction between surfaces not sliding relative to each other; adjusts up to a maximum μ_s N.
Friction between sliding surfaces, opposite to the relative velocity.
Net force toward the centre that a circular motion requires; supplied by tension, friction, gravity or a normal force.
A road tilted so the horizontal part of the normal force supplies the centripetal force at a design speed.
An accelerating or rotating frame; the laws of motion hold there only if inertial (fictitious) forces such as the centrifugal force are added.
Inertial force on a body moving relative to a rotating frame, perpendicular to its velocity; deflects winds and projectiles on Earth.
Resistance of a fluid to a body moving through it; grows with the square of speed for fast motion, linearly for slow motion in viscous fluid.
Constant speed reached when the drag force balances the weight.
Energy transferred by a force acting along a displacement; only the component of force along the path does work. SI unit the joule.
Energy of motion of a particle; depends on the frame through the speed.
Work done by the net force, equal to the sum of the works of all forces.
The net work done on a particle equals its change of kinetic energy.
Rate at which work is done; P = F⃗·v⃗ for a force acting on a moving body. Average power is work over elapsed time.
Energy of a system stored in its configuration; only differences are physical, so the zero can be chosen freely.
Potential energy of the body–Earth system for a height y near the surface.
Potential energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring.
A force whose work between two points is independent of the path; equivalently zero around every closed path, and derivable from a potential energy.
Work by forces such as friction or air resistance, which depends on the path and changes the mechanical energy.
Kinetic plus potential energy of a system.
Mechanical energy changes only through the work of nonconservative forces; without them it is a conserved quantity.
A plot of U(x) with the total energy as a horizontal line; motion is allowed only where E ≥ U, and reverses at turning points.
A position where the force vanishes; stable at a minimum of U (small disturbances oscillate), unstable at a maximum.
Mass times velocity; a vector.
Time integral of a force; for a short collision, average force times duration.
The impulse of the net force equals the change of momentum.
A chosen set of bodies; forces split into internal (between members) and external. A closed system has no net external force.
The total momentum of a closed system does not change, whatever happens inside it.
Collisions conserve momentum; they are classified by kinetic energy: elastic (kept), inelastic (lost), perfectly inelastic (bodies stick together), explosion (gained).
Mass-weighted average position of a system; for a continuous body r⃗_CM = (1/M)∫ r⃗ dm.
The centre of mass moves like a single particle of total mass M acted on by the external forces alone.
Mass per unit length of a rod or string; used to integrate over continuous bodies.
A rocket gains speed by ejecting mass backward at exhaust speed u; the gain depends on the logarithm of the mass ratio.

nodes.label: Rigid body on a fixed axis

extra.description: A body whose particles keep their mutual distances, turning about a fixed axis: every particle moves on a circle and one angle describes them all.
Angle of a reference line of the body from a fixed direction, in radians: arc length over radius.
Rate of change of angular position; as a vector it points along the axis by the right-hand rule. Tangential speed v_t = rω.
Rate of change of angular velocity; tangential acceleration of a point is a_t = rα.
Equations for rotation at constant angular acceleration, the same form as the linear ones with θ, ω, α in place of x, v, a.
Kinetic energy of a rotating rigid body, the sum of ½m_j v_j² with v_j = r_{j}ω.
Rotational inertia: how mass is distributed about the axis. Depends on the axis chosen.
The moment of inertia about any axis equals that about the parallel axis through the centre of mass plus Md².
Mass per unit area of a thin sheet or disk.
The turning effect of a force about a point or axis: force times lever arm, |τ| = r⊥F, signed by the right-hand rule.
Net torque about a fixed axis equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.
Work done by a torque as the body turns.
A wheel rolls without slipping when its contact point is instantaneously at rest; translation and rotation are then locked together.
Moment of momentum about a point; for a rigid body rotating about a symmetry axis, L = Iω.
The rate of change of angular momentum equals the net external torque.
With no net external torque, the total angular momentum is constant; a skater who pulls in her arms (smaller I) spins faster.
Slow turning of a spinning top's axis, because gravity's torque changes the direction of L⃗ rather than its size.
A rigid body at rest that stays at rest; it has no translational and no rotational acceleration.
The first condition (zero net force) prevents translation; the second (zero net torque) prevents rotation.
Point where the total weight can be taken to act; it coincides with the centre of mass in a uniform gravitational field.
Force per unit area that deforms a body: tensile or compressive (perpendicular), bulk (from all sides), shear (parallel to the surface).
Fractional deformation: change of length, volume or shear offset divided by the original size; dimensionless.
For small deformations stress is proportional to strain; the constant is the elastic modulus of the material for that kind of deformation.
Elastic modulus for tension or compression along one direction.
Elastic modulus for uniform compression; its inverse is the compressibility.
Elastic modulus for shear deformation.
Perpendicular force per unit area; a scalar. SI unit the pascal, 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
A material is linear up to the proportionality limit, elastic (returns to shape) up to the elastic limit, plastic beyond it, and breaks at the ultimate stress.
Strength of gravity between two masses, 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², first measured with a torsion balance (Cavendish).
Every pair of point masses attracts along the line joining them with a force proportional to both masses and inversely to the square of the distance.
Gravitational force per unit mass at a point; it exists whether or not a test mass is there.
What a scale reads: the normal force, which differs from mg in an accelerating or rotating frame (reduced at the equator by Earth's rotation).
Potential energy of two masses at any separation, with zero at infinite separation; near Earth's surface it reduces to mgy.
Minimum launch speed for a body to move off to infinite distance.
A system whose total energy is negative cannot separate to infinity; the bodies stay within a maximum distance.
Speed of a circular orbit at radius r; independent of the satellite's mass.
Time for one circular orbit.

extra.symbol: orbit = ellipse, Sun at a focus
extra.description: Every planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus; derived by Newton from the inverse-square law.
The orbital state: an ellipse traced periodically, closest to the Sun at perihelion and farthest at aphelion.
The line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fastest at perihelion.
The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semimajor axis.
Difference in the gravitational pull across a body; it stretches the body along the line to the attracting mass. Sun and Moon aligned give spring tides, at right angles neap tides.
Speed of light in vacuum, exactly 299 792 458 m/s by the definition of the metre (≈ 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s).
Gravity is the curvature of space-time produced by mass and energy; free bodies follow the straightest paths of the curved geometry.
No local experiment can distinguish a uniform gravitational field from an accelerated frame; a freely falling frame is locally inertial.
A mass compressed inside its Schwarzschild radius; nothing, not even light, escapes from inside the event horizon.
Radius at which the escape velocity from a mass M reaches the speed of light; it marks the event horizon.
A liquid or gas: matter that flows because it cannot resist a shear stress when at rest; described by fields such as density and pressure.
Mass per unit volume.
Density relative to that of water; dimensionless.
Gauges read pressure relative to the atmosphere; absolute pressure adds atmospheric pressure.
In a fluid at rest pressure grows with depth so that each fluid element is balanced: p = p₀ + ρgh for constant density.
A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid reaches every part of it; a hydraulic jack multiplies force by the area ratio.
Net upward force of a fluid on an immersed body.
A body immersed in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
A model fluid with constant density and no internal friction; its steady flow is laminar.
Internal friction of a fluid: the shear stress needed per velocity gradient.
The motion of a fluid: a velocity at every point. In laminar flow the layers slide smoothly; in turbulent flow eddies mix them.
Volume of fluid passing a cross section per unit time.
Mass entering a flow tube equals mass leaving; for an incompressible fluid A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so the flow speeds up where the tube narrows.
Along a streamline of an ideal fluid, pressure plus kinetic and potential energy per volume is constant; faster flow means lower pressure (Bernoulli's principle).
Laminar viscous flow through a tube: flow rate is the pressure difference over a resistance R = 8ηl/(πr⁴).
Dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous effects; flow in a tube is laminar below about 2000 and turbulent above about 3000.
Time for one cycle of a periodic motion (an oscillation).
Number of cycles per unit time; SI unit the hertz.
A mass on an ideal spring: the restoring force is proportional to displacement, giving simple harmonic motion.
The oscillator's state: amplitude A and phase shift φ about the equilibrium position; equivalently the pair (x, v) at one instant.
Stiffness of a spring: force per unit stretch, in N/m.
Force that pushes a body back toward a stable equilibrium point; linear for small displacements.
A point mass on a light string; for small angles it is a harmonic oscillator whose period depends only on length and g.
An extended body swinging about a pivot; its period depends on its moment of inertia and the distance L from pivot to centre of mass.
A body twisting on a wire whose restoring torque is proportional to the twist angle.
An oscillator with a drag force proportional to velocity; it is underdamped (decaying oscillation), critically damped or overdamped (no oscillation).

extra.symbol: mẍ + bẋ + kx = F₀ sin ωt
extra.description: A damped oscillator pushed periodically settles into motion at the driving frequency; its amplitude peaks (resonance) when the driving frequency is near the natural one.
A disturbance that travels through a medium (mechanical wave) while each part of the medium only oscillates about its equilibrium; transverse or longitudinal.
Distance between adjacent identical points of a periodic wave.
Speed at which the disturbance propagates; set by the medium, not by the source.
A wave shape that moves without changing; a pulse is a single such disturbance and y = A sin(kx − ωt + φ) is the periodic case.
Spatial angular frequency of a wave, in rad/m; v = ω/k.
The equation satisfied by every wave travelling at speed v in a linear medium.
Energy per unit time carried by a wave; proportional to the square of the amplitude and of the frequency.
Power per unit area carried by a wave; for a spherical wave I = P/(4πr²).
At a fixed end the displacement is zero and a reflected pulse is inverted; at a free end the slope is zero and the pulse returns upright.
Two overlapping waves add constructively (in phase, double amplitude) or destructively (half a cycle apart, cancel).
When waves overlap, the displacements add; follows from the linearity of the wave equation.
Two equal waves moving in opposite directions produce a pattern that does not travel: nodes stay at rest, antinodes oscillate most.
A string fixed at both ends can only hold standing waves that fit its length: the fundamental and its overtones.
A longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions in a medium; the pressure wave is a quarter cycle out of phase with the displacement wave.
Set by an elastic property over an inertial property of the medium: √(B/ρ) in fluids, √(Y/ρ) in solids, √(γRT/M) in an ideal gas.
Logarithmic measure of intensity relative to the threshold I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m².
Standing sound waves in a tube: open at both ends all harmonics f_n = nv/2L; closed at one end only odd ones, f_n = nv/4L.
Two sounds of slightly different frequency produce a loudness that rises and falls at the difference frequency.
The frequency heard changes when source or observer moves through the medium: higher when approaching, lower when receding.
A source faster than sound piles up its wavefronts on a cone; the pressure jump is heard as a sonic boom, and a boat's bow wake is the surface analogue.
How hot a body is, read from a thermometer; bodies in thermal equilibrium share one temperature. SI unit the kelvin.
The state reached by bodies in thermal contact when heat transfer between them has stopped.

extra.symbol: A ~ C, B ~ C ⇒ A ~ B
extra.description: Two bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other.
Celsius and Fahrenheit are relative scales; the Kelvin scale is absolute, with zero at absolute zero and the triple point of water at 273.16 K.
Most materials grow when heated: linearly in the temperature change for small changes; β ≈ 3α for isotropic solids. Water below 4 °C is an exception.
Stress that appears when a body is prevented from expanding or contracting.
Energy transferred between bodies because of their temperature difference. 1 cal = 4.186 J (mechanical equivalent of heat).
Heat needed per unit mass to raise the temperature by one kelvin.
Heat lost by the hot bodies in an insulated container equals heat gained by the cold ones.
Which phase (solid, liquid, gas) is stable at each pressure and temperature; the coexistence lines meet at the triple point and the liquid–vapor line ends at the critical point.
Heat absorbed or released at constant temperature during a phase change: heat of fusion, vaporization or sublimation.
Heat flows through a material at a rate proportional to area and temperature difference and inversely to thickness.
Heat transported by bulk motion of a fluid, driven by buoyancy (natural) or by pumps and fans (forced).
Every body radiates energy at a rate proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature; the net rate is σeA(T₂⁴ − T₁⁴).
For a dilute gas, pressure times volume is proportional to the number of molecules and the absolute temperature (Boyle, Charles and Gay-Lussac combined).
Converts temperature to energy per molecule: 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
Number of molecules in one mole, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; the mole counts amount of substance.
Boltzmann's constant per mole: 8.31 J/(mol·K).
Corrects the ideal gas law for attraction between molecules (a) and their own volume (b); predicts liquefaction below a critical temperature.
A gas in equilibrium is fixed by two of p, V, T; the third follows from the equation of state, so the state is a point on a pV diagram.
A gas is many point molecules in random motion; pressure is the momentum they transfer to the walls in collisions.
Total kinetic and potential energy of the molecules; for a monatomic ideal gas only kinetic, (3/2)Nk_BT.
Square root of the mean square molecular speed.
In a mixture each gas exerts its own partial pressure as if alone; the total pressure is their sum.
Average distance a molecule travels between collisions; divided by the mean speed it gives the mean free time.

nodes.label: Molar heat capacity at constant volume

extra.description: Heat per mole per kelvin at fixed volume.

extra.symbol: ½ k_B T per degree of freedom
extra.description: In thermal equilibrium each quadratic term in a molecule's energy (degree of freedom) carries an average energy ½k_BT.
The equilibrium distribution of molecular speeds in an ideal gas.
Speed at the peak of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution; below the mean and rms speeds.
A part of the world separated by a boundary from its surroundings (environment); closed if no matter crosses, open otherwise. In equilibrium a few variables describe it.
A relation among the state variables of a system in equilibrium.
A process slow enough that the system passes through a sequence of equilibrium states, so it is a curve on the pV diagram.
Work done by a system that changes volume; the area under the path on the pV diagram, so it depends on the path.
The change of internal energy equals the heat added to the system minus the work done by the system.

Paths with one quantity held fixed: T (isothermal), p (isobaric), V (isochoric), or no heat exchanged (adiabatic); a cyclic process returns to its start. A reversible process can be run backward through the same states.

nodes.label: Molar heat capacity at constant pressure

extra.description: Heat per mole per kelvin at fixed pressure; larger than C_V because the gas also does work.

nodes.label: Adiabatic process of an ideal gas

extra.description: In a quasi-static adiabatic expansion the gas cools; pressure and volume follow pV^γ = constant with γ = C_p/C_V.
A process that cannot be undone without leaving a change in the surroundings: friction, free expansion, heat flow across a finite temperature difference.

extra.symbol: no spontaneous heat flow cold → hot
extra.description: Heat never flows spontaneously from a colder to a hotter body; doing so requires work.
A device run in a cycle that takes heat Q_h from a hot reservoir, rejects Q_c to a cold reservoir and delivers the difference as work.
Fraction of the heat taken in that is turned into work.
An engine run backward: work moves heat from a cold reservoir to a hot one, to cool the cold side (refrigerator) or heat the hot side (heat pump).
Heat moved per work supplied; can exceed 1.
No cyclic process can convert heat from one reservoir entirely into work; equivalently there is no perfect engine (and, by the Clausius form, no perfect refrigerator).
A reversible cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic steps between two reservoirs; an engine run on it is a Carnot engine.
No engine between two reservoirs beats a reversible one, and all reversible engines between them have e = 1 − T_c/T_h.
A state function whose change is the heat added reversibly divided by the absolute temperature.
The entropy of an isolated system never decreases; it stays constant only for reversible processes.
Entropy changes along an isotherm vanish as the temperature approaches absolute zero; absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.
A property of matter that comes in two signs: like charges repel, unlike attract. Additive; SI unit the coulomb.
The total charge of an isolated system never changes; charging a body only moves charge from one body to another.
Ordinary charge is carried by electrons (−e) and protons (+e); neutrons are neutral. An ion has more or fewer electrons than protons.
A material in which some electrons (conduction electrons) move freely; charge placed on it spreads out, and nearby charges can induce a separation (charging by induction).
A material whose charges are bound to atoms; a field can only shift them slightly, polarizing the material into small dipoles.
Two point charges exert forces on each other along the line joining them, proportional to the product of the charges and inversely to the square of the distance.
Constant in Coulomb's law, 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²); k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
The force from several charges is the vector sum of the forces each would exert alone.
The simplest electrostatic state: which charges there are and where they sit.
The field produced by source charges, defined at every point of space; a test charge there feels qE⃗.
Force per unit test charge at a point; measured with a small test charge.
Charge spread along a line, over a surface or through a volume, described by a charge density; an infinite straight wire and an infinite plane are idealised cases.
Curves drawn tangent to the field, starting on positive and ending on negative charges, more crowded where the field is stronger.
Charge times separation of a ± charge pair; molecules can have a permanent dipole or one induced by a field.
The amount of field passing through a surface: field component along the area vector (normal to the surface) times area, summed over the surface.
The electric flux through any closed (Gaussian) surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀.
With spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry the field is constant on a well-chosen Gaussian surface, and Gauss's law gives it directly.
With charges at rest, the field inside a conductor is zero, excess charge sits on the surface, and just outside E = σ/ε₀ perpendicular to the surface.
Potential energy of a system of charges; the Coulomb force is conservative, so it exists.
Potential energy per unit charge at each point; a scalar field defined up to an additive constant.
Potential difference between two points, measured with a voltmeter; SI unit the volt. qΔV is an energy (electron-volt for q = e).
The vector of partial derivatives of a scalar field; points toward steepest increase.
Surfaces of constant potential; the field is perpendicular to them and no work is done moving a charge along one. A conductor's surface is one; grounding sets it to zero.
Two conductors carrying equal and opposite charges, often separated by a dielectric; the parallel-plate capacitor is the standard example.
Charge stored per volt of potential difference; depends only on geometry and the material between the conductors. SI unit the farad.
Capacitors in parallel share a voltage and their capacitances add; in series they share a charge and the inverses add.
Work needed to charge a capacitor, stored in its electric field.
Energy per unit volume stored in an electric field.
Factor by which an insulating material between the plates raises the capacitance and lowers the field.
The applied field induces or aligns molecular dipoles; the induced surface charges create an induced field that partly cancels the applied one.
Largest field an insulator withstands before it breaks down and conducts.
Rate at which charge passes a cross section; SI unit the ampere (1 A = 1 C/s). Conventional current points the way positive charge would move.
A closed conducting path through sources and elements, drawn as a schematic; charge flows steadily only around closed paths.
Small average velocity of the charge carriers along a wire, superposed on their fast random motion.
Current per unit area at each point of a conductor; integrated over a cross section it gives the current.
Material property: field needed per unit current density; its inverse is the electrical conductivity. It grows roughly linearly with temperature in metals.
Voltage per current of a component; for a uniform wire R = ρL/A. SI unit the ohm.
For many materials current is proportional to voltage with R independent of V (ohmic); devices such as diodes are nonohmic.
Rate at which electrical energy is delivered to an element; in a resistor it becomes heat at I²R = V²/R.
Below a critical temperature some materials lose all resistance and expel magnetic fields (Meissner effect); a quantum effect of electron pairs.
Work per unit charge done by a source (battery, generator) in moving charge around a circuit; the voltage of the source with no current.
Voltage across a source's terminals; below its emf by the potential drop on its internal resistance.
Resistors in series carry the same current and their resistances add; in parallel they share the voltage and the inverses add.
Junction rule: current into a junction equals current out. Loop rule: the potential differences around any closed loop sum to zero.

extra.symbol: series, small R / parallel, large R
extra.description: An ammeter is placed in series and has very small resistance; a voltmeter is placed in parallel and has very large resistance, so neither disturbs the circuit much.
A capacitor charging or discharging through a resistor: charge and current change exponentially with time constant τ = RC.
Every magnet has a north and a south pole; like poles repel, unlike attract, and cutting a magnet never isolates a single pole.

nodes.label: Magnetic force on a moving charge

extra.description: A charge moving through a magnetic field feels a force perpendicular to both its velocity and the field (right-hand rule); the force does no work.
The field around magnets and currents, mapped by a compass; its field lines form closed loops. SI unit the tesla (1 G = 10⁻⁴ T).
Field at one point, defined through the force on a moving test charge: B = F/(qv sin θ).
A charge in a uniform field moves on a circle of radius mv/(qB) with period 2πm/(qB); a velocity component along B⃗ turns the circle into a helix.
Current times area of a loop (times the number of turns), along the loop's normal; a current loop is a magnetic dipole.
Voltage across a current-carrying strip in a magnetic field, from carriers pushed to one side; its sign reveals the sign of the carriers.
Crossed electric and magnetic fields pass undeflected only particles with speed E/B.
Each element of a current contributes to the magnetic field in proportion to the current and inversely to the square of the distance, perpendicular to both element and line of sight.
Constant in the magnetic field laws, 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A.

nodes.label: Field of a long straight wire

extra.description: Circles around the wire, falling inversely with distance (right-hand rule for its direction).
Parallel currents attract and antiparallel currents repel; this force once defined the ampere.
The line integral of the magnetic field around any closed loop equals μ₀ times the current through it.
A long coil has a nearly uniform field inside, B = μ₀nI, and almost none outside; a toroid confines its field, B = μ₀NI/(2πr).
Atomic magnetic dipoles respond to a field: weakly along it (paramagnetic, χ > 0), weakly against it (diamagnetic, χ < 0), or strongly with domains and hysteresis (ferromagnetic).
Amount of magnetic field through a surface; SI unit the weber.
A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an emf in it, whether the field, the area or the orientation changes.
The induced emf drives a current whose magnetic field opposes the change of flux that produced it.
Emf in a conductor moving through a magnetic field.
A changing magnetic field creates an electric field whose lines close on themselves; it is not conservative.
Currents induced in a conductor moving in, or exposed to, a changing magnetic field; by Lenz's law they oppose the motion (magnetic damping).
A coil turning in a magnetic field produces a sinusoidal emf with peak NBAω; a motor's coil produces the same, called back emf.
Flux through one circuit per current in another; a changing current in one induces emf ε₂ = −M dI₁/dt in the other. SI unit the henry.
A coil's own flux per unit of its current; a changing current induces ε = −L dI/dt that opposes the change. An inductor is a coil built for this.
Work done against the back emf while the current builds up, stored in the magnetic field.
Energy per unit volume stored in a magnetic field.
Current in a resistor–inductor circuit rises or decays exponentially with time constant τ_L = L/R.
Charge sloshes between a capacitor and an inductor; energy passes between electric and magnetic fields.
Adding resistance damps the LC oscillation: underdamped, critically damped or overdamped as for a mechanical oscillator.
A source whose voltage (and current) reverses periodically; direct current (dc) flows one way only.
Represents a sinusoid A sin(ωt + φ) as a vector of length A rotating at ω; sinusoids of one frequency add as vectors.
Opposition of a capacitor to alternating current; current leads voltage by 90°.
Effective values of a sinusoid: the dc values that deliver the same average power.
Opposition of an inductor to alternating current; current lags voltage by 90°.
Total opposition of a series RLC circuit to ac, I₀ = V₀/Z; the phase angle φ = tan⁻¹((X_L − X_C)/R) is how far current lags voltage.
Power averaged over a cycle; only the resistor dissipates, and cos φ is the power factor.
Current in a series RLC circuit peaks when X_L = X_C; the quality factor measures how sharp the peak is (bandwidth Δω = ω₀/Q).
Two coils on one iron core: the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, and the current ratio its inverse, so power is transmitted at high voltage and low current.
Gauss's law for E⃗, Gauss's law for B⃗ (no monopoles), Faraday's law, and Ampère's law with Maxwell's displacement current; with the Lorentz force they complete classical electromagnetism.
Maxwell's term: a changing electric flux acts like a current in Ampère's law, needed where a capacitor interrupts the conduction current.
The dynamical state of classical electromagnetism: electric and magnetic fields at every point and time, evolving by Maxwell's equations.
A solution of Maxwell's equations in empty space: transverse electric and magnetic fields in phase, travelling at c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀).
Energy flux of the electromagnetic field: energy per unit area per unit time, along the direction of propagation.
Pressure exerted by light because electromagnetic waves carry momentum U/c.
Electromagnetic waves of all wavelengths: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, distinguished only by frequency.
Ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in a medium; at least 1.
Geometric optics: light travels along straight rays in a uniform medium, bending only at boundaries. Valid when objects and apertures are much larger than the wavelength.
A ray reflects from a smooth surface at the same angle to the normal as it arrived, in the same plane.

extra.symbol: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
extra.description: A ray entering a medium of different index bends toward the normal if the new index is larger (Snell's law).
Angle of incidence beyond which light going into a medium of lower index is totally reflected (total internal reflection).
The index of refraction depends on wavelength, so a prism spreads white light into colours.
Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets; the new wavefront is their envelope. It explains reflection, refraction and diffraction (wave optics).
The direction of the electric field of light in the plane perpendicular to its travel: fixed for polarized light (vertically, horizontally…), random for unpolarized light.
A polarizing filter transmits the field component along its axis, so intensity falls as cos²θ.
Angle of incidence at which reflected light is completely polarized parallel to the surface.
Where rays from a point of an object meet (real image, can be caught on a screen) or appear to come from (virtual image). A plane mirror forms a virtual image as far behind as the object is in front.
For a curved (spherical) mirror and rays near the optical axis, object and image distances are related through the focal length f = R/2.
Image height over object height; negative for an inverted image.
Real mirrors and lenses do not bring all rays to one point: spherical aberration (rays far from the axis), coma (off-axis points), and others.
A single spherical boundary between media forms images; for a flat boundary it gives the apparent depth h_i = (n₂/n₁)h_o.
Two refracting surfaces close together: converging lenses (f > 0) and diverging lenses (f < 0), with 1/f = (n₂/n₁ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) (lens maker's equation). Images are found by ray tracing.

nodes.label: The eye as an optical system

extra.description: The eye images onto the retina at fixed distance by changing its power (accommodation) between the near and far points; myopia and hyperopia are corrected with lenses.
Inverse focal length in diopters (m⁻¹); powers of thin lenses in contact add.
How much larger an object appears through an instrument than to the unaided eye at the near point; a simple magnifier gives at most 1 + 25 cm/f.
Two-lens instruments: the objective forms a real image that the eyepiece magnifies; magnifications multiply.
Light waves whose phase difference stays constant (coherent), usually of one wavelength (monochromatic); incoherent light washes out interference.
Young's experiment: light from two slits forms bright fringes where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths (order m) and dark fringes halfway between.
With N slits the principal maxima stay at d sin θ = mλ but become sharper, with N − 2 weak secondary maxima between them.

Light reflected from the top and bottom of a thin film interferes; a half-wavelength phase change on reflection from a higher-index medium decides which colours are reinforced (soap bubbles, Newton's rings).
Splits a beam, sends the halves along two arms and recombines them; moving one mirror by λ/2 shifts the pattern by one fringe.
Light spreads after passing a narrow slit; wavelets from different parts of the slit cancel at angles where a sin θ = mλ.
Intensity across the single-slit pattern, β = πa sin θ/λ; the central peak's width is set by λ/a.
With slits of finite width, the double-slit fringes are modulated by the single-slit envelope; fringes falling on envelope minima are missing orders.
Thousands of equally spaced slits give very sharp principal maxima, so a grating separates wavelengths precisely.
Two point sources are just resolved when the central maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other; diffraction limits every optical instrument's resolution.
X-rays reflected from successive planes of atoms in a crystal (Bragg planes) interfere constructively when the extra path 2d sin θ is a whole number of wavelengths.
A hologram records the interference of object light with a reference beam, storing amplitude and phase; illuminated again, it reconstructs a three-dimensional image.
Einstein's theory of space and time for inertial frames, built on two postulates; it reconciles mechanics with electromagnetism.

extra.symbol: same laws in all inertial frames
extra.description: The laws of physics, including electromagnetism, have the same form in every inertial frame.
An interferometer turned relative to Earth's motion showed no change in the speed of light: there is no detectable motion through an ether.

extra.symbol: c the same in all inertial frames
extra.description: Light in vacuum travels at c in every inertial frame, whatever the motion of source or observer.

extra.symbol: t_A = t_B in S ⇏ in S′
extra.description: Two events simultaneous in one inertial frame are generally not simultaneous in another moving relative to it.
A clock moving relative to an observer runs slow: the time between two events at one place in the clock's frame (proper time Δτ) is the shortest.
Factor that measures how far relativistic effects depart from Newtonian ones; 1 at rest, infinite at c.
A body is longest in its own rest frame (proper length L₀); measured while it moves, it is shorter along the motion, L = L₀/γ.

extra.symbol: x′ = γ(x − vt),  t′ = γ(t − vx/c²)
extra.description: Converts the coordinates of an event between two inertial frames so that the speed of light is the same in both.
The four-dimensional arena of special relativity; a particle's history is a world line, and the interval between events is the same in all frames.
Velocities combine so that no sum of speeds below c ever exceeds c; for slow speeds this reduces to classical (Galilean) velocity addition.
The frequency of light from a receding source is lower (red shift), from an approaching one higher; it depends only on the relative velocity.
The momentum conserved in all inertial frames; m is the rest mass, the same in every frame.
Work needed to bring a body from rest to speed u; it grows without bound as u → c, so no massive body reaches c.
Total energy of a body: kinetic energy plus its rest energy mc²; mass is a form of energy. E² = (pc)² + (mc²)².
Radiation in equilibrium with a perfect absorber and emitter at temperature T; its spectrum depends only on T, peaking at λ_max with λ_max T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K (Wien).
The quantum of action, 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; it sets the scale at which energy comes in discrete amounts.
The oscillators exchanging energy with cavity radiation can only have energies that are whole multiples of hf.
Light on a metal ejects photoelectrons (photocurrent from the photoelectrode); their maximum kinetic energy is measured by the stopping potential.
Below a cut-off frequency (above a cut-off wavelength) no electrons are emitted, however intense the light.
A quantum of the electromagnetic field: energy hf, momentum h/λ along the propagation vector, zero rest mass. The photoelectric effect is a quantum phenomenon.
Minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal's surface.
X-rays scattered by electrons come out with longer wavelength, by an amount fixed by the scattering angle; λ_c = h/(m₀c) = 0.00243 nm is the Compton wavelength.
Hydrogen emits and absorbs only at discrete wavelengths (Fraunhofer lines in sunlight), in series named Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund and Humphreys.
Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed that nearly all of an atom's mass and its positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus, with electrons far outside.
Postulates for hydrogen: the electron moves only on orbits with angular momentum nħ, does not radiate on them, and emits or absorbs a photon when it jumps between them.
The allowed states of Bohr's atom: radii r_n = a₀n² (Bohr radius a₀ = 0.529 Å) and energies −E₀/n²; ground state −13.6 eV, ionization energy 13.6 eV. Hydrogen-like ions scale with Z.
Every particle has an associated matter wave (de Broglie wave) with wavelength h/p; the wave packet moves at the group velocity, which equals the particle's velocity.
Davisson and Germer saw electrons diffracted by a nickel crystal with the angles of Bragg's law, confirming λ = h/p.
Light and matter both show wave behaviour (interference in the double-slit interference experiment) and particle behaviour (single detections); neither picture alone suffices.
Position and momentum cannot both be sharp: the product of their uncertainties is at least ħ/2.
The quantum state of a particle: a complex function of position and time; its symmetry under x → −x may be even or odd.
|Ψ(x, t)|² is the probability density for finding the particle at x; the total probability is one (normalization condition).
A measurement gives one definite outcome, and the wave function is then replaced by one consistent with it (wave function collapse, Copenhagen interpretation).
Average of many measurements on identically prepared systems; position and momentum act as operators x and −iħ ∂/∂x.
In the limit of large energies (large quantum numbers) quantum predictions agree with classical mechanics.
A localised wave made by superposing plane waves of nearby wave numbers; the narrower it is in x, the broader in k.
A state that lasts only Δt has an energy spread at least ħ/(2Δt); short-lived states have broad lines.
The equation of motion of the wave function: given Ψ at one time and the potential energy U, it fixes Ψ at all times.
For a potential that does not change in time, Ψ = ψ(x)e^{−iωt}; ψ satisfies an eigenvalue equation for the energy, and e^{−iωt} is the time-modulation factor.

A particle confined to an infinite square well: ψ_n = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L), standing matter waves; only discrete energy levels with quantum number n ≥ 1 are allowed, so even the ground state energy is nonzero.
A solution with one definite energy; its probability density does not change, so it is a standing wave state.
The Schrödinger equation with U = ½mω²x²: equally spaced levels, a zero-point energy ħω/2, and wave functions built from Hermite polynomials.
A particle can cross a potential barrier higher than its energy; the transmission probability falls exponentially with barrier width and with √(U₀ − E).

Solutions of the Schrödinger equation for the Coulomb potential: atomic orbitals labelled by n, l (0 … n − 1) and m (−l … l). Energies depend only on n and agree with Bohr's; electrons have no definite orbits.
Magnitude and one component of orbital angular momentum take only discrete values.
The orbiting electron is a current loop; its moment comes in units of the Bohr magneton μ_B = eħ/2m_e.
In a magnetic field, levels with different m split, and spectral lines split into several components.

Intrinsic angular momentum of the electron, s = ½ with m_s = ±½, shown by the two beams of the Stern–Gerlach experiment; it carries a magnetic moment μ⃗_s ≈ −(e/m_e)S⃗, antiparallel to the spin because the electron's charge is negative.
The electron's spin moment interacts with the field of its orbital motion (fine structure) and with the nuclear spin (hyperfine structure, spin-flip transitions such as hydrogen's 21-cm line).
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of quantum numbers (n, l, m, m_s).
Electrons fill subshells in order of energy, each with at most 4l + 2; the outermost (valence) electrons fix chemical groups and the transition metals.
Atomic transitions that emit or absorb a photon change l by one, because the photon carries one unit of angular momentum.
Heavy atoms emit characteristic X-ray lines when an inner vacancy is filled, with frequencies following Moseley's law; a continuous braking-radiation spectrum accompanies them.

An incoming photon stimulates an excited atom to emit an identical photon; with more atoms in an excited metastable state than below it (population inversion) the light is amplified into coherent, monochromatic light.

Atoms bind by transferring an electron (ionic bond, energy set by ionization energy, electron affinity and Coulomb attraction), by sharing a pair of electrons in an antisymmetric spin state (covalent bond, exchange symmetry, hybridization), or by induced dipoles (van der Waals bond).
A diatomic molecule rotates and vibrates with quantized energies; electric dipole transitions obey Δl = ±1 and Δn = ±1, giving band spectra.

Atoms or ions in a solid arranged in a repeating lattice (simple cubic, body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic); the Madelung constant sums the Coulomb energy of an ionic crystal, and a repulsion constant sets the short-range repulsion.

Conduction electrons as particles in a three-dimensional box, filling the lowest states two per level (exclusion principle) up to the Fermi energy; occupation at temperature T follows the Fermi factor.

In a crystal the atomic levels broaden into energy bands separated by energy gaps; a filled valence band with a large gap gives an insulator, a small gap a semiconductor, a partly filled band a conductor.
Impurity atoms add donor levels (n-type, extra electrons) or acceptor levels (p-type, holes) in the gap; the majority carrier sets the type, and the Hall effect shows its sign.
Joining p- and n-type material creates a depletion layer with a built-in field; current flows easily in forward bias and hardly at all in reverse bias, until breakdown.
Two junctions back to back: a small base current controls a large collector current, so the device amplifies.
Field above which superconductivity is destroyed; type I superconductors switch abruptly, type II pass through a mixed state.
Lattice vibrations bind electrons into Cooper pairs, which condense into one quantum state that carries current without resistance.
A nucleus specified by its atomic number Z (protons) and neutron number N; mass number A = Z + N counts nucleons. Isotopes share Z. Radius r = r₀A^{1/3}; masses in atomic mass units.
Attraction between nucleons, much stronger than the Coulomb repulsion at about 1 fm but negligible beyond a few fm.
Energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons, equal to the mass defect times c²; binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron.
Unstable nuclei decay at random with a constant probability λ per unit time, so their number and activity fall exponentially: half-life T½ = 0.693/λ, mean lifetime 1/λ.
Ages from the fraction of a radioactive isotope left, as in carbon-14 dating of once-living material.

A parent nucleus becomes a daughter: α decay emits a helium nucleus, β⁻ decay an electron and an antineutrino, β⁺ decay a positron (antielectron) and a neutrino, γ decay a photon from an excited nucleus. Heavy nuclei decay in series; transuranic elements are made artificially.
A heavy nucleus such as ²³⁵U splits after absorbing a neutron, releasing about 200 MeV and further neutrons; a chain reaction is critical when each fission causes one more on average (critical mass).
Treats the nucleus as a drop of incompressible nuclear fluid held by surface tension (strong force) and pushed apart by Coulomb repulsion; deformation splits a heavy drop.
Light nuclei combine and release energy; in the Sun four protons become helium by the proton–proton chain. Stars build heavier elements (nucleosynthesis).
Energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue (rad), weighted by the relative biological effectiveness of the radiation to give the equivalent dose (rem, sievert).

Four fundamental forces, each carried by bosons: gluons (strong), photons (electromagnetic), W and Z bosons (weak), gravitons (gravity, unobserved). The electromagnetic and weak forces unify into the electroweak force; grand unified theories and a theory of everything are sought.

Matter is made of fermions (half-integer spin): leptons such as the electron and neutrino, and quarks, which form hadrons (baryons from three quarks, mesons from a quark and an antiquark). Every particle has an antiparticle, such as the positron. Bosons carry the forces.
Reactions conserve charge, baryon number and lepton number; strangeness is conserved by the strong and electromagnetic forces but not the weak force.
Hadrons are built from quarks with fractional charges; a new quantum number, color, lets three identical quarks share a state, and only colourless combinations exist.

The theory of the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces: forces arise from the exchange of virtual particles, pictured in Feynman diagrams; quantum electrodynamics (QED) and quantum chromodynamics (QCD) are its parts.
Distant galaxies recede with speeds proportional to their distance, measured from the redshift of their light; H₀ is Hubble's constant.
The universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense early state; cosmology studies this history.
Radiation left from the hot early universe, now a nearly uniform blackbody spectrum at 2.7 K in the microwave range.
Galaxies rotate too fast for their visible mass (dark matter), and the expansion is accelerating (dark energy); together they make up most of the universe's energy.
